title: Read: katakana, step by step
description: The second script. Mostly used for foreign words like ice cream and hotel.

units.title: The five vowels
intro: Katakana is the second Japanese script. It has the same 46 sounds as hiragana, just written with sharper, straighter shapes.
It is mostly used for words borrowed from other languages: hotel, coffee, America. Names of foreign people and places are written in it too.
So you already know every sound. This path is about learning a new set of shapes for them. Start with the five vowels: a, i, u, e, o.
Katakana is drawn with straight strokes and sharp corners. Hiragana is curvy. That is the quickest way to tell them apart.

items.hint: Looks like an axe: 'ah!' as it hits the log.
Two strokes, a short slash and a post, like an eel on a stick. 'ee'.
Two dashes on a cap with a hook below, like a surprised face going 'ooh'.
Like a capital I: an elevator shaft, 'eh'.
A cross bar with a slash through it, like a person with open arms going 'oh!'.

units.title: The K row
intro: The K row in katakana: ka, ki, ku, ke, ko.
Careful with ク and ケ. ク has no vertical post. ケ has one. Also compare ク with タ from a later unit: タ has an extra stroke.
ケ and コ both look square and tidy. コ is just two lines forming a corner.

items.hint: Like the hiragana か without its extra dot: a blade and a hook, 'ka'.
A key with three teeth: 'ki' for key.
Like an open-mouthed bird beak, angled. 'ku' as in 'cool'.
Looks like a capital K made of straight lines, with a post. 'ke' as in 'kept'.
A corner, like the letter L turned over. Two lines, 'ko'.

units.title: The S row
intro: The S row in katakana: sa, shi, su, se, so.
Same surprise as hiragana: the second one is 'shi', not 'si'.

Big trap coming: シ (shi) and ソ (so) look nearly the same, and so do ツ (tsu) and ン (n) later. The difference is the angle. シ has two short dashes and a long sweep that goes up. ソ has one dash and a long stroke that goes down.

items.hint: Three strokes, like a sail on a boat. 'sa'.
Three strokes, two dots on the left lying flat and a sweep rising: 'she smiles', lying on her side.
A horizontal bar with a hook that bends: a snake on a rock. 'su' as in 'sue'.
Looks like a seat with a back, a bit like it fell over. 'se' as in 'set'.
A dash and a long stroke going down, like a stitch of sewing thread: 'so'.

units.title: The T row
intro: The T row in katakana: ta, chi, tsu, te, to.
Remember the surprises: the second one is 'chi' and the third is 'tsu'.
ツ (tsu) and シ (shi) are twins. ツ has its two dashes on top, pointing down. シ has them on the left, lying flat. Tsu stands tall, shi lies down.

items.hint: Like ク with one more stroke through it, like a 'ta'-ble with a leg: 'ta'.
Three strokes: a short bar, a cross-bar, and a long hook, like a chair. 'chi' as in 'cheese'.
Three strokes, two dashes on top and a sweep: tsunami waves coming down.
A telephone pole with two cross-bars. 'te' as in 'ten'.
A post with a small stick leaning on it, like a toe. 'to'.

units.title: The N row
intro: The N row in katakana: na, ni, nu, ne, no.
ノ (no) is just one slanted stroke, the simplest katakana of all. It is part of many others, like メ and ア.
ヌ (nu) and ス (su) look alike. ヌ has an extra stroke crossing the hook.

items.hint: A cross with a slash through it, like a knife: 'na' as in 'nacho'. Careful: メ (me) has no bar on top.
Two lines, one above the other, like the number 2. 'ni' sounds like 'knee', and ni also means 'two' in Japanese.
Like ス with an extra stroke across the hook, like noodles being pulled. 'nu' as in 'noodle'.
A dash on top of a hooked post with a small tail, like a fishing net on a pole: 'ne'.
One slash from top right to bottom left. 'no'.

units.title: The H row
intro: The H row in katakana: ha, hi, fu, he, ho.
Again 'fu' is a soft f: blow air between your lips, no biting.
ヘ (he) is almost the same as the hiragana へ. Learn them as one shape. ホ (ho) looks like a tree with a cross-bar.

items.hint: Like the roof of a house with a left and a right slope: 'ha'.
Like a hook on a post, as if hoisting a flag: 'hi'.
A flat roof over a hook, like a fur hood. 'fu'.
The same shape as hiragana へ: one little hill. 'he' as in 'hen'.
A tree with a cross-bar and two small leaves, like 'ho ho ho', Santa's tree.

units.title: The M row
intro: The M row in katakana: ma, mi, mu, me, mo.
メ (me) looks like ノ crossed by another line, a bit like an X. Do not mix it up with ナ (na): ナ has a horizontal bar on top.

items.hint: A triangle with a stroke inside, like a map of mountains: 'ma'.
Three slanted lines, like three fingers held up: 'mi' for 'me, me, me'.
A small triangle with a tail, like a cow's head saying 'moo': 'mu'.
Two strokes crossing like an X: the eye of a needle, 'me' for eye.
Like the hiragana も made of straight lines: two bars and a hooked post, 'mo'.

units.title: The Y row
intro: The Y row in katakana has only three: ya, yu, yo.
ユ (yu) looks like a corner with an extra line. Careful: コ (ko) is just a corner, ユ has a long tail.

items.hint: A cross with a drooping arm, like a yak with its head down: 'ya'.
A corner shape that looks like a U with a flat bottom: 'you'.
Three horizontal lines hanging off a post, like a yo-yo string: 'yo'.

units.title: The R row
intro: The R row in katakana: ra, ri, ru, re, ro.
Same soft Japanese r as before, a quick tap of the tongue, between r, l, and d.
ロ (ro) is a plain square. ル (ru) has two legs, and the right one has a hook.

items.hint: A dash on top of a hooked line, like a rack with a hat. 'ra'.
Two vertical lines, the right one hooked. 'ri' like 'ree'.
A post with a hook on the right and a long leg on the left, like a person walking: 'ru'.
A single hook on a post, like the letter L slanted: 're' as in 'red'.
A plain square, like a road sign: 'ro'.

units.title: The last three
intro: Three characters left: wa, wo and n. After this you can read all 46 basic katakana.
ヲ (wo) is said 'o'. It is hardly used in katakana, so we skip its listening test.
ン (n) and ソ (so) look alike. ン is nearly horizontal on its left: the dash points down and to the right in a flat angle. ソ looks like it is falling.
ワ (wa) looks like ウ (u) without the top dash.

items.hint: Like ウ without the dash on top: a wide mouth, 'wa'.
Said 'o'. Almost never used in katakana. Just recognize it.
Two strokes: a dash and a sweep that lies flat, like a person lying on their side saying 'n'.
